title: Look What Sits in This Word
subtitle: On the fire that was burning before anyone was there to see it
teaser: The first word of the Bible has six letters. The outer four spell covenant. The two in the middle spell fire. Nobody is claiming Moses put it there. But it is sitting there.
theme: The fire you are trying to get back was lit before you arrived, by Someone who loved first
framework: Genesis 1:1 — In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth

modules.passage: We love because He first loved us.
modules.scriptureContext: Five words that set the order of everything else. Not a reward for loving. The reason we can.

modules.definition: in the beginning; in the first, the chief, the choicest part
modules.usage: The opening word of the Hebrew Bible. It is built from the preposition בְּ (b', "in") joined to רֵאשִׁית (reshit, "beginning"), which comes in turn from רֹאשׁ (rosh, "head"). So the Bible opens, quite literally, at the head of things.
modules.usageNote: Six letters carry it: bet, resh, aleph, shin, yod, tav. Hold that shape in mind. We come back to it below.

modules.heading: The Order Nobody Chooses
modules.content:
John does not write that God loves us back. He writes that God went first.

That sounds gentle. It is not. It removes something from you. If God loved first, then your love is not the cause of anything. It is a response. You are answering a voice that was already speaking.

Most of us learned it the other way around. Reach hard enough and heaven leans in. Pray well enough and something opens. That arrangement is exhausting, and it has one advantage we rarely admit out loud: it keeps us in charge. If my effort starts the fire, my effort controls it.

John takes that away. And what he puts in its place is stranger and better. The fire in you was lit by somebody else. You did not strike it. You will not restart it by striking harder.

This matters most on the days you feel nothing. If your love began the relationship, then a cold week is evidence against you. If His love began it, a cold week is just a cold week. The thing it rests on has not moved.

We are at the very beginning of the story this week. Creation. Before the fall, before the promise, before the exile. Before anyone had done anything at all, good or bad, God was already the one moving first.

There is a second thing it does, quieter than the first. It takes shame out of the equation.

If love is a response, then the gap between what you feel and what you think you should feel is not a verdict on you. It is just a gap. It can be honestly reported instead of hidden. People who believe they must generate the warmth learn very early to perform it, because the alternative is admitting the fire is low. And a person performing warmth cannot be reached.

Going second is a relief. It means you are allowed to arrive cold.

modules.prompt: Think of one thing you have been trying to feel your way back into with God. Now ask it differently: what if that thing was never yours to start?

modules.heading: A Two-Minute Prayer
modules.prayerText: Father, You loved first. Before I knew, before I answered, before I could have earned a single thing. Let that be the ground I stand on today, and not my own warmth. Amen.

modules.ctaSubtext: That can be the whole of today. Below, when there is time: the six letters of the Bible's first word, what a medieval rabbi noticed sitting inside them, and why John opens his Gospel with the same three words as Genesis.

modules.passage: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
modules.scriptureContext: Seven words in Hebrew. The whole library rests on them. And the very first word is the one we are going to look at.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A scribe's hands on a blank hide scroll, a reed pen held between fingers and thumb, warm light glowing outward through the parchment fibres from behind the page
modules.inlineImageCaption: The light is behind the page, not on it — which is the argument of the whole day.

modules.heading: Six Letters
modules.content:
Hebrew is written in consonants. Vowels came later, added by scribes who wanted to preserve how the words had always been said. That means a Hebrew word is a run of letters, and sometimes a run of letters holds a shape its author never put there.

Here is the first word of the Bible: בְּרֵאשִׁית. Six letters. Bet, resh, aleph, shin, yod, tav.

Take the outer four — the first two and the last two. Bet, resh, yod, tav. That spells בְּרִית, *b'rit*. Covenant.

What is left in the middle is aleph and shin. אֵשׁ, *esh*. Fire.

Covenant, wrapped around a flame.

Now let us be careful, because this is the kind of thing people oversell and then get caught. This is not the word's etymology. *Bereshit* is simply "in" plus *reshit*, "beginning," which comes from *rosh*, "head." The split we just made cuts straight across the grammar. It takes a preposition, half a root, and a suffix, and throws away the middle of the root. No one who studies Hebrew for a living would call that a derivation. Nobody is claiming Moses encoded it.

But it is not ours either. A medieval midrash noticed it long before we did and wrote it down: bet and resh are the head of the word, yod and tav are the end, and that is *b'rit*. What remains is aleph-shin, and that is *esh*.

So we are not decoding a secret. We are doing what readers of this text have always done. We are looking at a word long enough to see what is sitting inside it.

Two more objections are worth meeting before someone raises them for you.

The aleph in reshit is quiescent. It is written but not sounded. So reading it as the aleph of esh is something you do with your eyes, not your ear. And the yod in both words is what grammarians call a vowel letter — it is doing a vowel's job, not a root consonant's.

Both of those are true. Neither one touches the observation. Nobody is claiming these words share a root. The claim is only that the letters, as written on the page, sit in that order. They do. You can count them.

Which is a useful habit generally. Say the smaller true thing. It survives.

modules.usage: A primitive word. That is a technical term, and it means something worth knowing: *esh* is not built from anything older. It has no root behind it. Hebrew simply arrives with a word for fire already in hand.
modules.usageNote: Its neighbour in this word is בְּרִית (b'rit), H1285, covenant. And the lexicons derive *b'rit* from a root meaning to cut — a compact made by passing between pieces of flesh. Hold on to that. Tomorrow we watch it happen.

modules.content: The fire is not something the covenant produces. It is something the covenant is wrapped around.

modules.heading: The Same Three Words
modules.content:
Now turn to the front of John's Gospel.

"In the beginning was the Word."

A first-century reader would not have heard that as a nice opening line. They would have heard a quotation. Those are the words Genesis starts with, and John has picked them up deliberately and set them down again at the head of his own book.

Genesis says: in the beginning, God made. John says: in the beginning, the Word was. And then John does the thing that turns the whole library over. He says the Word was with God, and the Word was God. And a few lines later he says the Word became flesh.

So the Word is not a text. The Word is a Person.

This is why we cannot treat two things as separate jobs this week. There is the work of getting your relationship with God warm again. And there is the work of getting back into Scripture. Most of us feel those as two chores, and both of them feel heavy.

John will not let them stay separate. The Word you are avoiding is not a book that describes Him. It is Him. Opening it is not homework you do so that a relationship can happen later. It is the relationship, happening.

That cuts both ways, and the uncomfortable side is worth saying plainly. If you have been reading and reading and feeling nothing, you have not failed at a technique. You may simply have been treating a Person like a manual.

There is one more move in John's opening that is easy to read past. He does not only say the Word was God. He says the Word was with God.

With. A preposition doing enormous work. It means the Word was not a function God performed or an attribute God possessed. There was company there, before there was anything else to keep company with.

So relationship is not something God started once He had made someone to have it with. It is what He already was. When you are invited into it, you are not being given a new arrangement. You are being brought inside an old one.

modules.videoTitle: What It Means for Jesus to Be the "Word of God"
modules.videoCaption: Shows why John opens with "In the beginning" — he is deliberately reaching back to Genesis 1 to say the Word who made the world has become a Person.

modules.heading: Then and Now
modules.ancientTruth: A scribe copying Genesis worked in consonants only, with no vowel marks and no spaces the way we use them. He looked at every letter individually because he had to. Getting one wrong meant starting the sheet again.
modules.modernApplication: We read fast, in translation, on a screen, usually while something else is loading. It is not a moral failing. It is just a different relationship to the page — and it makes a word like this one invisible.
modules.connectionPoint: The pattern in bereshit is not hidden. It is simply too small to survive the speed we normally read at.
modules.newTestamentEcho: Which may be why Jesus so often answers a question with "Have you not read?" — asked of people who had, in fact, read it.

modules.heading: Fire You Did Not Light
modules.content:
There is a reason this is where the week starts.

If you are here at all, something in you has gone quiet. Maybe it is prayer that has thinned out into a habit. Maybe it is a season that changed underneath you — a job, a house, a family shape — and the faith that fit the old season does not seem to fit this one. Maybe you sat down with a study and could not finish it, and the not-finishing has become its own small shame.

The instinct in that state is to try to generate heat. Read more. Feel more. Be more disciplined about it.

Genesis will not let us start there. Before anything is asked of anyone, God is already at work in a dark and formless place. Nothing had earned that. Nothing had asked for it. The very first thing the Bible tells you about God is that He moves first, into a situation that has nothing to offer Him.

And John says: that same One walked into a room and had a face.

So the fire this week is not a fire you are being told to produce. It was lit before you were there to see it. The covenant it sits inside was made without your signature. The love that started it went first, and it went first specifically so that nothing about it would depend on how you feel this morning.

That is either the most freeing sentence in the book or the most insulting one, depending on how badly you want to be the one who made it happen.

Most of us want that more than we admit. Being loved first is lovely in theory. In practice it means arriving somewhere you did not build, at a table you did not set, and being handed a seat.

This lands hardest on people in the middle of a change.

When the shape of a life shifts, the practices that carried your faith usually shift with it. The commute where you prayed is gone. The friends you talked about it with are somewhere else now. The hour that used to be quiet belongs to something new. And because the practices went quiet, it is easy to conclude that the thing underneath them went quiet too.

It usually did not. What went is the scaffolding, not the building. Those are very different losses, and mistaking one for the other has ended more faith than doubt ever has.

Genesis is unbothered by formlessness. It is the opening condition, not the emergency.

modules.heading: A Woman Teaching Her Children Under the Sky
modules.content:
In Ulster County, New York, near the end of the eighteenth century, a woman known as Mau-mau Bett was enslaved on the Ardinburgh farm. She had ten or twelve children. Most had been sold before her youngest daughter could remember them.

When the owner died, the girl — Isabella, who would take the name Sojourner Truth much later — began finding her mother crying. She asked why. Her mother said she was thinking of the children who had been sold away.

Then, under the night sky, Mau-mau Bett gathered the children she still had and taught them. She spoke in Low Dutch, the only language she had.

"My children, there is a God, who hears and sees you." The children asked where he lived. "He lives in the sky," she said, "and when you are beaten, or cruelly treated, or fall into any trouble, you must ask help of him, and he will always hear and help you." She taught them to kneel and say the Lord's Prayer.

Isabella was sold at nine years old for one hundred dollars, in a lot with sheep.

Decades later she was still praying that prayer in Low Dutch, as taught her by her mother. She did not light that. It was handed to her, in the dark, by a woman with almost nothing left to hand anyone.
modules.connectionToTheme: A fire lit by someone else, in conditions that should have made it impossible, still burning long after the one who lit it was gone.

modules.heading: One Honest Note About That Story
modules.content:
Sojourner Truth could not read or write. The account above comes from a book dictated to Olive Gilbert and published in 1850, written down in the third person, in Gilbert's English. Truth sold it herself at her lectures for the rest of her life, so it is her authorized account. That is a real claim, and it is a slightly different claim from these being her words.

It is worth saying plainly, because the whole point of this week is a fire that gets handed from one person to another. Some of the handing is visible in the record. Some of it we only have secondhand. That does not make it less real. It makes it like most inheritance.
modules.historicalContext: Olive Gilbert, Narrative of Sojourner Truth, Boston, 1850. Truth was called Isabella Baumfree until 1843; every event above happened under that name.

modules.heading: What This Week Is Actually Asking
modules.content:
So here is the shape of the next six days.

Tomorrow we watch God make a promise to a man who is asleep for it. On the third day we find the word this week is named after, and it turns out to be a word Paul used exactly once, written to somebody young and frightened whose faith had come to him from his grandmother. Then a day about coming to the fire as a lamb rather than as its keeper. Then a day about lamps going out, which is the honest part. Then we gather it, and then we rest.

None of those days will ask you to work up a feeling.

What they will ask is smaller and harder. They will ask you to stop treating your own warmth as the measurement. To notice that the thing you are trying to restart has been burning in the dark the whole time, kept by Someone who does not need you awake to keep it.

Start there today. Not with effort. With the order of operations.

He loved first. Everything else in this week — every lamp, every altar, every hand cupped around an ember — is downstream of that one sentence.

One practical note before you go.

You do not need to finish this week to have gotten something from it. That sounds like permission to quit. It is not. It is a description of how this particular fire behaves — it does not require an unbroken streak, and the day you skip is not a reset.

Say that out loud now, at the start, because on about day four most people miss one and quietly stop.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A vast empty expanse above a dark sea, the horizon low in the frame, one small point of warm light sitting on the line
modules.inlineImageCaption: Genesis opens over dark water with nothing in it yet — and something is already moving.

modules.passage: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
modules.scriptureContext: Chosen in the King James here for one reason: it opens with exactly the same three words as its Genesis translation, so the echo John built is visible on the page instead of buried in a paraphrase.

modules.prompt: Somebody handed you whatever faith you have — a parent, a friend, a stranger, a book. Who was it, and have you ever actually thanked them?
additionalQuestions: Where did you first get the idea that your relationship with God depends on how much heat you can produce?
If the fire was lit before you arrived, what changes about the mornings you feel nothing?
Is there a difference, for you, between reading Scripture and meeting a Person? What would it take to close it?

modules.heading: A Breath to Carry Today
modules.instruction: This one is short on purpose. Say the first line as you breathe in, the second as you breathe out. Do it four or five times, slowly, and then stop.
steps: Repeat four or five times, unhurried.
Then let it go and get on with your day. Nothing more is required of it.

modules.heading: Before You Close This
modules.content:
One word. Six letters. Covenant on the outside, fire in the middle.

It is not proof of anything. It will not win an argument. It is closer to a thing you notice on a wall you have walked past a thousand times, and once you have seen it you cannot stop seeing it.

And it is a decent picture of what this week is about. The fire is real. It is small. It is surrounded on every side by an agreement you did not negotiate, made by Someone who went first, and it has been there since the first word of the first sentence.

You do not have to feel it today. It is not asking you to.

Tomorrow a man falls asleep at sunset, and God walks through the dark alone.

modules.inlineImageAlt: An open doorway in a thick dark mud-brick wall, warm light falling outward across the ground toward the viewer and stopping at their feet, nobody standing in it
modules.inlineImageCaption: The light comes out to where you are, and there is no one in the doorway asking you to prove anything.

modules.heading: Closing Prayer
modules.prayerText:
God of the beginning,

Before there was anything to love, You were already moving over the dark. Before I knew Your name, You knew mine. I did not start this and I cannot end it.

I have spent a long time trying to be warm enough to deserve You. I am tired of it. Teach me the other order — Yours first, mine after.

And where the fire in me has gone quiet, let me stop striking at it long enough to notice it never actually went out.

In the name of the Word who came and stood in a body. Amen.
modules.breathPrayer: You loved first / I am answering

modules.heading: Carry This
modules.commitment: I will stop measuring my standing with God by how much I feel today.
leavingAtCross: The belief that I have to generate the warmth before God will meet me
The idea that a cold morning is evidence against me
The quiet pride of wanting to be the one who made it happen
receivingFromCross: A fire I did not light, inside a covenant I did not sign
An order of operations where His move comes first

modules.heading: Check Yourself
modules.question: The letter pattern inside bereshit is best described as which of these?
options: A modern invention with no history behind it
A real pattern in the consonants, noticed by Jewish tradition, but not the word's etymology
A hidden code deliberately placed there by Moses
modules.explanation: All three parts matter. The letters genuinely spell b'rit around esh. A medieval midrash recorded it centuries ago, so it is not something we made up. And it is not the etymology — bereshit is b' plus reshit, from rosh. Claiming more than that is where people get caught.

modules.heading: Who Wrote This Down
modules.name: The compiler of Midrash Aggadah
modules.era: Medieval; recovered from an Aleppo manuscript and first printed by Solomon Buber, Vienna, 1894
modules.bio: We do not know who assembled this collection. What we have is a manuscript that surfaced in Aleppo and was edited and published in the nineteenth century. Its comment on Genesis 1:1 sets out the letter pattern exactly as it appears above.
modules.keyQuote: Bet, resh — the head of the word. Yod, tav — the end of the word. And that is covenant.
modules.lessonForUs: The reading is old, but it is medieval rather than ancient, and its own point was different from ours — it took the fire to mean Torah. Naming that honestly costs nothing and keeps the observation standing.
